turn_text: So first of all, it's been severe. It's been the worst drought that I think we've been on the farm. My wife and I, this is our 44th harvest coming up here. It's going to be probably the smallest harvest we've ever had because of the drought. And then we got hit with a hailstorm last Sunday. I'll be cutting Friday, by the way. So five days before harvest, which is, I mean, that's agriculture. That's production agriculture. You take the good with the bad and it's been a painful year. And I will tell you east of me where I'm in the north central part of the state east of me. I don't know that the grass even greened up in the eastern part of Montana. It's been that dry. And so they're going to cut even less than we're going to. And I will tell you that we've been talking to Secretary Vilsack. And he's been very responsive to us so far to be able to allow emergency hang and grazing on CRP, for example. And then to be honest with you there, they're going to have to gear up because there's, you know, we got crop insurance, we got hail insurance, but it doesn't seem to be ever enough. And so we're going to be pushing, you know, as we move forth here, we're going to be pushing to make sure that we're supporting our family farm agriculture people, whether you're in the ranching business or in farming, to make sure that they're around it. It's important for our food chain, it's important for rural markets, I think it's important for food security. We don't want these folks going broke. And I think years like this, even though, you know, if you've been at this game long enough, you know, you try to salt away a little money during good times because, you know, every year isn't going to be a diamond. And this is one of those years, it's a stone. And we're going to need some, we're going to need to have the federal government have our backs. And we'll be pushing Secretary Vilsack to do exactly that.
